wiki-iran.standing: Daily readership of the English Wikipedia article on Iran — a rough gauge of how many people worldwide are looking the country up rather than a measure of anything happening inside it.
wiki-iran.recent: The window's peak came before the current sanctions round; the low on Aug 15 preceded it. Attention has since tracked the Hormuz standoff and Treasury's "Economic Outcast" campaign, which named nearly 60 entities Monday and drew Iran's Rezaei to warn that "not even one drop" leaves Hormuz. The rial opened at 2.02 million per dollar.

brent.standing: The price of a barrel of North Sea crude, and the benchmark most of the world's oil is priced against. It moves on supply — a strike, a sanction, a strait — and fuel, freight and fertiliser move after it.
brent.recent: Brent sits near $95 after a run from $68.53 on Jul 2 to $105.30 on Jul 23, with the Strait of Hormuz at the centre of it. Iran's Rezaei warned that "not even one drop" would leave Hormuz, and one gas carrier transited on Monday; Treasury Secretary Bessent named his Iran sanctions campaign "Economic Outcast.

wti.standing: The US benchmark crude grade, priced at Cushing, Oklahoma and the reference for most North American oil contracts. It sets what refiners pay for a barrel, and petrol, diesel and freight costs follow it.
wti.recent: Oil ran to $99.76 on Jun 3 and slid to $69.60 by Jul 6 before turning back up: the expiry of the 60-day US-Iran MoU deadline pushed crude above $91 by 18 August, with Hormuz traffic falling to single digits and Karachi's KSE-100 down 2,547 points. Prices then retreated as China cut oil imports 45%.

natgas-hh.standing: The US benchmark price for natural gas, set at a Louisiana pipeline hub and used to price most American gas contracts. It sets what power stations, heating bills and fertiliser plants pay, and it anchors the cost of US LNG sold abroad.
natgas-hh.recent: Gas has drifted down across the window, from $3.34 in late May to $2.82, with the floor at $2.56 on 7 August. The supply news since has run the same direction: Iran reported 161 billion cubic meters recoverable in Fars province, and Pakistan Petroleum struck gas in Chiltan rock at Sujawal.

wheat.standing: The world benchmark price for a tonne of milling wheat, the grain that feeds more people directly than any other. It moves on harvests, export policy and the safety of the Black Sea, and bread prices follow it.

rice.standing: The world price of milled rice, the staple grain for more than half the planet and the one most exposed to export bans. Asian harvests and Indian trade policy set the level; a single restriction can reprice food across West Africa and the Gulf.
rice.recent: The series sits near the bottom of its two-year range, down from the Aug 2024 high of 563.8 to 464 by Jul 2026, with a floor of 330.6 in Oct 2025. Nothing in the record explains the drift. In the background, research in Bangkok raised Jasmine rice yields with two bacteria strains, and an Australian court backed Pakistan over India on Basmati.

copper.standing: The price of a tonne of refined copper, the metal that carries electricity in almost everything that uses it. Grids, motors, buildings and data centres all compete for the same supply, and mine output is slow to respond.
copper.recent: The series peaked at 13,550 $/mt in Jun 2026, roughly 50% above its Dec 2024 low of 8,910. Demand for electrification runs through the same metal: AI-driven transformer redesign, EV charging that strains grid voltage in London, and a UK rollback of EV targets. Zambia, a major producer, reelected Hakainde Hichilema on a copper and debt-restructuring platform.

us-10y.standing: The yield on ten-year US government debt, the price at which the world's largest borrower funds itself. It is the reference rate under mortgages, corporate loans and asset prices almost everywhere, so when it moves the cost of long-dated money moves with it.
us-10y.recent: The series climbed to 4.75% on 31 July from 4.38% on 26 June, and the yield sits near 4.7%. What the coverage names is a Treasury preoccupied with other business: Secretary Bessent's "Economic Outcast" sanctions campaign on Iran, and traders in New York pricing yield-curve control hopes off a buyback. Neither explains the move in the yield itself.

sp500.standing: A capitalisation-weighted index of 500 large US-listed companies, and the default measure of American equity performance. Pensions, index funds and retirement accounts worldwide track it, so its level sets the paper wealth of savers far beyond the US.
sp500.recent: The index sits near the top of its two-month range, 1.5% above where it started and just off the 7,799 high on Aug 13. Fed minutes on Aug 19 showed many officials saying rate hikes may be needed, and Treasury yields rose on strong services data; Walmart's Aug 20 slide gave retail stocks a fresh problem while AI names held up, with Nvidia pledging $500 billion to its own buyers.

nasdaq100.standing: A stock index tracking the 100 largest non-financial companies on the Nasdaq exchange, weighted by market value. Chipmakers, cloud providers and platform companies dominate it, so it moves as a bet on technology earnings rather than the broad economy.
nasdaq100.recent: The index sits below its Jun 2 high of 30660 after bottoming at 27190 on Jul 29, with the questions that drove it still open. Nvidia beat estimates and guided to $108bn in revenue next quarter, but disclosed it backstops $230 billion in customer lease obligations and pledged $500 billion to its own buyers. Meta took a $17.1bn child-safety settlement and scrapped a plan to cut some teams by 60%.

us-gas-retail.standing: The average price American drivers pay at the pump, surveyed weekly across the country. It follows crude, but the gap between the two is refining: when refineries or pipelines falter, pump prices move even when a barrel does not.
us-gas-retail.recent: Fuel markets spent August short of refining, not crude. Ukrainian drones hit Russian plants and Moscow capped station sales at 30 litres, while Putin conceded "not all fuel issues have been resolved" and Russia moved to import fuel and lower standards. India cut its windfall tax on petrol exports to nil, easing supply elsewhere.

natgas-ttf.standing: The price of natural gas at the Dutch TTF hub, the benchmark for gas traded in northwest Europe. It sets what factories, power stations and households pay for heat and electricity, and it moves on pipeline supply, storage levels and weather.
natgas-ttf.recent: The series is monthly and runs to 1 July 2026, so it predates the month's gas news: it rose 47% from a December 2025 low of $9.46 to $17.93 in July, its highest in the window. The coverage since — a second Nord Stream sabotage suspect arrested in Croatia, and Iran's Fars province find of 161 billion cubic meters — postdates the reading.

vix.standing: A measure of how much movement traders expect in the S&P 500 over the coming month, derived from options prices. It rises when investors pay up for protection, which is why it is read as a gauge of fear in American equity markets.
vix.recent: The index sits near the calm end of its three-month range, having drifted down from the June high to a low of 14.25 on Aug 14 before edging back to 15.85. Volatility has left both crypto and traditional markets even as U.S.-Iran risks linger and sovereign debt rises, with rising yields and Brent crude dragging equities lower.

fx-pkr.standing: Pakistan's currency, quoted as rupees to the dollar, and the price at which a country that imports most of its fuel, edible oil and machinery pays for them. A weaker rupee reaches consumers through the pump and the grocery bill before it reaches anyone's spreadsheet.
fx-pkr.recent: The rupee has been close to flat over the month, easing from 278.1 on Aug 7 to 277.2 while the pressures on the import bill stayed local rather than monetary: a war-risk levy tied to Hormuz pushed diesel to 383.95 rupees a litre, and Sindh set out to import 5 million tons of wheat.

fx-ngn.standing: Nigeria's currency, quoted against the dollar. Africa's largest oil producer is also a heavy importer of fuel and food, so the naira's level sets domestic prices for both — and every devaluation passes through to the pump and the market stall.
fx-ngn.recent: The naira has been close to flat over the month, easing from 1,367 on Jul 28 to 1,346 by Aug 21 and 1,347 now. Nigeria's Centre for the Promotion of Private Enterprise made the case for why that steadiness is not the whole story: "Macroeconomic stability is a means, not an end." Atiku Abubakar's pledge to restore the petrol subsidy in 2027 puts the fiscal side of that stability back in contention.

fx-egp.standing: The exchange rate between Egypt's currency and the US dollar. Egypt imports most of its wheat and fuel, so the rate sets the domestic price of bread and energy, and it governs what the country's dollar debts cost to service.
fx-egp.recent: The pound has been close to flat over the month, easing from 51.16 on Aug 1 to 50.43, with a low of 49.56 on Aug 8. Nothing in the month's Egypt news explains the drift: Cairo hosted Gaza mediation talks and reopened a de-escalation channel with Tehran, neither of which touched the currency.

fx-try.standing: Turkey's currency, quoted as lira per US dollar, so a rising number means a weaker lira. Years of low policy rates against high inflation have made it one of the world's most persistently depreciating currencies, and import, energy and debt costs follow it.
fx-try.recent: The lira drifted to a fresh low of 48.11 on Aug 26, up about 1.6% from 47.37 on Jul 28 — a slow slide rather than a shock. Nothing in the month's Turkey news explains it: the story flow was diplomatic and military, from the Mecca defence pact with Pakistan and Saudi Arabia to the arms transfer to Ukraine that Moscow said undermines trust.

fx-bdt.standing: The exchange rate of Bangladesh's currency against the dollar. The country's garment exports are priced in dollars and its fuel, wheat and machinery are bought in them, so the rate sets what imports cost and what remittances from abroad are worth at home.
fx-bdt.recent: The taka has been steady through a political transition, easing from 124 on Aug 7 to 122 on Aug 19 before settling near 122.9. Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir was elected president on 21 August, and a government panel is now drafting terms for up to 24 J-10CE jets from China — a post-election Dhaka balancing India, China and the US.

fx-idr.standing: Indonesia's currency, quoted as rupiah per US dollar, so a higher number means a weaker rupiah. Southeast Asia's largest economy prices its commodity exports and dollar-denominated debt through it.
fx-idr.recent: The rupiah has firmed about 2% over the month, from 18,110 on Jul 28 to 17,650 on Aug 21, settling near 17,720. The coverage does not explain the move: Jakarta's news in the window was Prabowo's tightening state grip on the economy, a ruling that gig drivers are "partners" rather than employees, and RCEP's persistent capital gap.

fx-lbp.standing: The Lebanese pound's exchange rate against the US dollar. After the currency lost most of its value in Lebanon's banking collapse, the peg was reset far below its old level, and the rate now sets the cost of nearly everything in a country that imports most of what it consumes.
fx-lbp.recent: The pound has been close to flat for a month, drifting a quarter of a percent between its Jul 31 low of 89,180 and its Aug 7 high of 89,720, while the war outside the currency continued: Lebanon's health ministry put the death toll from Israeli attacks at 4,350, and a strike near Ansar killed seven on 15 August.

fx-cny.standing: The exchange rate between China's currency and the US dollar, managed within a band the People's Bank of China sets each morning. A weaker yuan makes Chinese exports cheaper abroad and imported commodities dearer at home, so it is watched as a signal of policy intent as much as of trade.
fx-cny.recent: The yuan strengthened to 6.721 per dollar on Aug 26, its firmest in the 30-day window and up from 6.772 on Jul 29. The coverage does not name a driver for the move; the currency news in the period concerns Beijing tripling the number of digital yuan banks to 30, and Pakistan asking Washington for $10 billion in dollars rather than renminbi.

fx-inr.standing: The rupee's price against the US dollar, the rate at which India's imports of oil, electronics and machinery are settled. A weaker rupee raises the cost of everything India buys abroad and eases the terms for its exporters and IT services.
fx-inr.recent: The rupee held in a narrow band through August, easing to 95.23 from a high of 95.78 on Jul 29 and a low of 95.05 on Aug 5 — a move of under half a percent across the month. Nothing in the period explains a directional shift: New Delhi's airport privatisation and Piyush Goyal's 200-firm trade delegation to Japan are structural, not currency, events.

fx-brl.standing: The exchange rate of Brazil's real against the US dollar. Brazil is a major exporter of soy, iron ore, beef and oil, and the real moves with commodity prices, the domestic interest rate and the fiscal outlook — a currency traders treat as a proxy for emerging-market risk.
fx-brl.recent: The real drifted weaker over the month, touching 5.222 on Aug 15 before recovering to 5.147. The month's Brazil news pointed to the longer-term energy story rather than anything moving the currency: Petrobras detected signs of oil off the Amazon coast, and Lula called the equatorial margin find a "passport.

fx-mxn.standing: Mexico's currency against the US dollar, one of the most heavily traded emerging-market currencies and a liquid proxy for US trade and border policy. Manufacturing supply chains, remittances and cross-border investment all price through it.
fx-mxn.recent: The peso firmed through August, reaching 16.92 on Aug 21 after a Jul 28 high of 17.46. Washington cancelled Andrés Manuel López Beltrán's US visa on Aug 14, drawing a rebuke from Claudia Sheinbaum, but the friction stayed political rather than commercial and the currency held its gains.

fx-eur.standing: The exchange rate between the euro and the US dollar, the most traded currency pair in the world. It prices trade between the two largest economic blocs, and moves mainly on the gap between what the European Central Bank and the Federal Reserve do with interest rates.
fx-eur.recent: The euro drifted down about 2.5% over the month, from 0.8792 on Jul 28 to a low of 0.8556 on Aug 20. The coverage in this window is regulatory and legal rather than monetary — EU sanctions plans, packaging and crypto rules, a Nord Stream arrest — and none of it explains the currency's move.

fx-jpy.standing: Japan's currency, quoted as yen per dollar, so a rising number means a weaker yen. It is the funding leg of the world's largest carry trade, which makes it a barometer of global risk appetite as much as of Japan's own economy.
fx-jpy.recent: The yen has firmed roughly 3 percent over the past month, from 163.8 on Jul 28 to 159, with the low of 156.5 on Aug 3. Nothing in the month's news accounts for the move: the events out of Japan were the torrential rains that killed 8, Putin's visit to the disputed Kuril Islands and the protest that followed, and an Indian trade delegation of 200 firms.

fx-rub.standing: The exchange rate of Russia's currency against the US dollar, quoted as rubles per dollar, so a higher number means a weaker ruble. It is the cleanest read on how sanctions, oil revenue and war spending are landing on Russia's economy.
fx-rub.recent: The ruble slid to 83.65 per dollar, weakening roughly 7% over the month and touching 85 on Aug 18, as Kremlin sources declared the peace talks dead and Moscow moved to let the state seize undefended factories. Treasury named nearly 60 entities on Monday, tightening the bind on third countries.

fx-zar.standing: The currency of South Africa, and the most heavily traded currency in Africa. It is a proxy for emerging-market risk appetite and for the metals the country digs up, so it swings on commodity prices and on foreign capital far more than on domestic trade.
fx-zar.recent: The rand strengthened through August, reaching 15.92 on 26 August after peaking at 16.78 on 28 July. Nothing in the domestic news of the period explains the move: the run of South African stories covers gang killings in Cape Town, R88.6bn in unclaimed accounts and pensions, and NSFAS improperly funding 40,000 students.

btc.standing: The largest cryptocurrency by market value, priced against the dollar and traded continuously worldwide. It has no yield and no issuer, so its price is almost purely a measure of how much demand there is to hold it — which makes it a fast, noisy read on appetite for risk.
btc.recent: Bitcoin climbed from $62,800 on Aug 2 to $79,010 on Aug 26, and the rally was driven by positioning rather than new buyers: $48 billion of open futures interest sat against $25 billion in daily volume, and the squeeze unwound into a 23.7% weekly surge. BlackRock then cut its swap-in threshold from $25 million to $1 million.

eth.standing: The native token of the Ethereum network, the largest platform for programmable contracts and the settlement layer most stablecoins and tokenised assets run on. Its price is a bet on how much of that activity keeps flowing through it.
eth.recent: The rise came alongside a rulemaking scramble in Washington: the SEC scrapped its Reg Crypto vote on 16 August, then proposed a full crypto rulebook a week later, while Cuomo lobbied for the Clarity Act. Money followed the licensing regimes rather than the open ones — $11.2 billion in six months, none of it permissionless.

paxg.standing: A token backed one-for-one by allocated London Good Delivery gold, so its price tracks bullion rather than crypto risk. It is the metal people buy when they distrust currencies, banks or governments — a store of value with no counterparty to fail.
paxg.recent: Gold ran 14% higher over the month to a $4,676 peak on Aug 25, and the physical trade shows the strain: in Kassala, street dealers now outbid the licensed market, and traders shut shop amid clashes and an illicit parallel market. Tether's KPMG audit, down to counting its gold bars by hand, landed in the same window.

wiki-artificial-intelligence.standing: A count of how many people open Wikipedia's article on artificial intelligence each day. It rises when the technology moves from trade press to general news, so it tracks public curiosity rather than anything about the technology itself.
wiki-artificial-intelligence.recent: The mid-August peak sat between two funding stories: Alibaba selling $10 billion in new shares for AI rather than spending cash, and Nvidia backstopping $230 billion in customer lease obligations. Readership then held near its high as Bill Gates reversed his January stance on AI and jobs, and Meta scrapped planned cuts of up to 60% in some teams.

wiki-russia.standing: Daily readership of the English Wikipedia article on Russia, a rough gauge of how many people worldwide are looking up the country rather than a measure of anything happening inside it.
wiki-russia.recent: The 17 August peak came on a day of compounding Russia stories: a strike on Koloskovo in Belgorod that killed six, including a 14-year-old; wildfires reaching the Chelyabinsk site where a 1957 tank blast dumped 20 million curies; and the EU foreign affairs chief pressing to expand sanctions. Putin's visit to the disputed Kuril Islands, which drew a Japanese protest, landed the following day.

wiki-pakistan.standing: Daily readership of the English Wikipedia article on Pakistan, a country of some 240 million people whose politics, security and economy draw attention far beyond its borders. Traffic rises when the country is in the news and falls back when it is not.
wiki-pakistan.recent: A fire in the nursery at PIMS in Islamabad killed fourteen newborns on 26 August, carried by more than five hundred outlets. The weeks before brought a contested election in Azad Jammu and Kashmir that protesters call a sham, Moody's two-notch upgrade to B3, and a joint defence pact signed with Saudi Arabia and Turkey whose text is not public.

wiki-china.standing: The English-language Wikipedia article on China, and a daily count of how many people open it. Readership on a country page moves with events rather than with the country, so the series works as a rough gauge of where global attention lands.
wiki-china.recent: The peak on 13 Aug sits before the run of stories that followed: Beijing ordered a recall of 3 million Teslas over flush door handles, a defect standard 60% of China's best-selling EVs share; China delayed its crewed Moon landing citing "ensuring absolute success"; and a flash flood at Rasuwagadhi on the Nepal-China border killed at least 160.

wiki-strait-of-hormuz.standing: The sea lane between Iran and Oman through which the Gulf's oil and gas must pass, a channel narrow enough that a single hull or a single mine can price the cargo behind it. What transits it sets what the rest of the world pays for energy.
wiki-strait-of-hormuz.recent: Readership tracked the closure of the strait: the 18 August peak followed an unknown projectile striking a vessel's engine room and killing one crew member, after traffic had already fallen to six ships on Tuesday. Iran's Rezaei then warned that "not even one drop" would leave Hormuz, and by Monday a single gas carrier transited.

wiki-india.standing: The Wikipedia article on India, the world's most populous country, and one of the most-read country pages on the site. Its daily readership rises and falls with whatever draws outside attention to the country — an election, a disaster, a diplomatic row.
wiki-india.recent: The peak on Aug 15 fell on Independence Day, when Modi renewed his push for 'aatmanirbhar Bharat' around semiconductor plants and energy security. Readership then eased through a week of smaller domestic stories — a temple stampede in Bihar that killed 7, and US envoy Sergio Gor's remark that J&K is an 'important part of India', which Pakistan summoned him over.

wiki-israel.standing: Wikipedia's article on Israel, and how many people open it each day. Readership is a rough gauge of public attention: it climbs when the country is at the centre of a story and settles back when it is not.
wiki-israel.recent: Attention tracked a widening campaign across three borders. Armoured vehicles expelled 20 UN refugee-agency staff at Qalandia on Tuesday, and Lebanon's agriculture ministry found glyphosate at 50 times normal levels in the soil of Ayta ash-Shaab. Earlier, eight strikes hit the same Idlib runway hours after four already had.

wiki-ukraine.standing: A daily count of how many people open the English Wikipedia article on Ukraine. It rises when the war forces itself back into general view, which makes it a rough gauge of outside attention rather than of the fighting itself.
wiki-ukraine.recent: The late-August rise tracked the air-defence crisis: allies convened in Kyiv on 24 August, where Zelenskyy said Patriot deliveries have halved since 2023, days after Russian missiles killed at least 13 in Kyiv. Britain then removed its veto on MBDA sharing SCALP component data with Ukraine.

wiki-nigeria.standing: Africa's most populous country and its largest economy, a federation of over 200 million people split between a Muslim north and a Christian south. It exports crude oil, imports refined fuel, and its politics turn on who controls both.
wiki-nigeria.recent: Attention fell back from its late-July peak through a month of local stories: Adeleke's re-election in Osun, which civil society groups said cost 14 deaths across 56 incidents; Atiku Abubakar's pledge to restore the petrol subsidy if he wins in 2027, which the APC called desperation; and Tinubu's suspension of three permanent secretaries over a fake agency.

cp:hormuz.standing: One-fifth of global seaborne oil passes through this 21-mile strait between Iran and Oman.
cp:hormuz.recent: Traffic has collapsed to a single gas carrier a day, down from six on 19 August, after mines and a projectile strike on a ship's engine room made the crossing uninsurable. Trump declared the strait cleared, and Iran and Oman have since agreed a temporary corridor — but Rezaei has threatened to let "not even one drop" leave.

cp:bab-el-mandeb.standing: Between Yemen and Djibouti — the Red Sea’s southern gate. Houthi attacks since 2023 have pushed container shipping to reroute around Africa.
cp:bab-el-mandeb.recent: Traffic sits near an eleven-year-low band and roughly a tenth below its own 90-day baseline, with the calmest seas offering no excuse. Houthi missiles have widened past the strait itself: one struck a Saudi supertanker off Yanbu on 24 August, and Saudi Arabia shelled Razih district villages in Saada the same day. Maersk, routing around the closure, raised profit guidance to $6.5 billion.

cp:suez.standing: Egypt’s 120-mile artery carries roughly 12% of global trade. The 2021 closure disrupted supply chains for weeks; Red Sea instability keeps it volatile.
cp:suez.recent: Traffic is running near its own 90-day baseline, up 2.6 percent over the last week, but the daily count has swung between 22 vessels on Jun 16 and 57 on Aug 11. Attacks on Red Sea shipping continue: the Houthis said they struck a vessel off Saudi Arabia on 24 August, and Pakistani nationals injured in an earlier Houthi attack returned home this month.

cp:malacca.standing: Between Malaysia and Sumatra — the fastest route between the Indian and Pacific Oceans. Over 80,000 ships a year, including most of China’s oil imports.
cp:malacca.recent: Traffic has run about 8% below its own 90-day baseline, easing from 264 vessels a day on Jun 22 to a low of 170 on Jul 19, with calm seas throughout. Nothing in the window accounts for it: the disruptions — Hormuz traffic falling to single digits, a Houthi missile hitting a Saudi supertanker off Yanbu — all sit far to the west.

cp:taiwan.standing: Between mainland China and Taiwan — roughly 40% of the world’s container traffic passes through, and the flashpoint of any US–China confrontation.
cp:taiwan.recent: Traffic is running about 3.7% below its 90-day baseline, at 225 vessels a day, with a swing from 28 on Jul 10 to 401 two days later. Nothing in the record explains the gap; waves peaked at 1.4m and no weather alert was in force.

cp:panama.standing: 50-mile shortcut between the Atlantic and Pacific. Drought in 2023–24 cut daily transits by half — a live example of climate binding to trade.
cp:panama.recent: Transits are running about a fifth below the mid-July peak of 83 vessels a day and roughly 13 percent under the canal's own 90-day baseline, with 28 on 23 August. The coverage does not explain the fall; the drought reporting in this window is European — the Rhine at Nijmegen and the Danube at Cernavoda, where low water shut a reactor — not Panamanian. A separate dispute is live at the canal's ports, where CK Hutchison is seeking HK$11.7b from Panama.

cp:bosporus.standing: Istanbul’s 20-mile waterway links the Black Sea to the Mediterranean — the only route for Russian naval access and Ukrainian grain exports.
cp:bosporus.recent: Traffic has run about 6% below its 90-day baseline as attacks on shipping mounted: three Greek vessels burned in the Black Sea in as many days to 18 August, and TASS said Russia had struck 130 ships since July. Turkey's MFA said it was not in contact with Moscow on any Black Sea moratorium.

cp:gibraltar.standing: 8 miles between Morocco and Spain — the only Atlantic–Mediterranean link. A surveillance chokepoint for Russian submarines and sanctioned oil.
cp:gibraltar.recent: Traffic has drifted down about a tenth over the window, from 163 vessels on Jun 13 to 119, and the last week runs 5.9% below the 90-day baseline. Waves peaked at only 0.9m, so weather is not the cause; the input names no closure or rerouting that explains the decline.

cp:dover.standing: The busiest shipping lane on Earth — 400+ ships a day squeeze through the English Channel’s 21-mile narrows.
cp:dover.recent: Traffic held near its own baseline, running about 6.5% below the 90-day average over the past week, with a high of 186 vessels on Aug 1 and a low of 126 two days later. Seas stayed calm, with a maximum wave height of 1.4 metres and no weather alert.

cp:cape-of-good-hope.standing: The 3,000-mile detour around southern Africa — the alternative when the Red Sea is closed. The new default for tankers since Houthi attacks began.
cp:cape-of-good-hope.recent: Traffic has held near its 90-day baseline, ending the window at 84 vessels a day, with a low of 68 on 27 July and a high of 123 on 31 July. Attacks on shipping have continued — a Houthi missile hit a Saudi supertanker off Yanbu on 24 August — but nothing in the window explains the swing around the route itself.

cp:kerch.standing: Between Crimea and Russia — the only access to the Sea of Azov. A flashpoint since 2014 and contested throughout the Russia–Ukraine war.

mkt:tadawul.standing: The Arab world’s largest exchange by market value, dominated by Aramco. Trades Sunday to Thursday, so it opens the global week before Tokyo.
mkt:tadawul.recent: The index closed at its 36-day high on Aug 26, the day a US-Saudi nuclear deal emerged without an enrichment ban, awaiting only Saudi recognition of Israel. Riyadh had also signed a joint defence pact with Pakistan and Turkey, though its terms stay undisclosed, while Houthi attacks on shipping and Saudi shelling in Saada continued.

mkt:bist.standing: Türkiye’s only exchange. Priced in lira, so its index level carries the country’s inflation as much as its earnings — read the direction, not the number.
mkt:bist.recent: The index sits near the top of its three-month range after a run of foreign-policy news: a joint defence pact signed by Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey, US missiles routed to Ukraine via Turkey over Moscow's objections, and Israeli strikes on the Idlib airbase that Israel said followed Syria's acceptance of Turkish troops.

mkt:dfm.standing: The Gulf’s main listing venue for property and banking. Moved from a Sunday–Thursday week to Monday–Friday in 2022, unlike Riyadh.
mkt:dfm.recent: The index sits well below its Jun 18 high of 6270 after Iran fired two ballistic missiles at the UAE on 18 August, triggering Dubai's first emergency alert in months, and the UAE responded by suspending all trade and financial transactions with Iran. Two ADNOC tankers were struck transiting Hormuz days earlier, and 137,000 Gulf tourism jobs are forecast lost.

mkt:bursa-malaysia.standing: The world’s largest market for Islamic finance instruments, and the centre of the global sukuk trade.
mkt:bursa-malaysia.recent: The index sits near the top of its 64-day range, having climbed from 1,657 on Jul 1 to a high of 1,749 on Aug 26 before easing. Nothing in the window explains the move.

mkt:idx.standing: The exchange of the world’s largest Muslim-majority country, heavily weighted to commodities and banking.
mkt:idx.recent: The index has climbed roughly a fifth off its June low and touched 6,526 on Aug 21, with the rise running alongside Prabowo's tightening state grip on the economy — a presidential imprint now reaching across the cooperatives and much else. Jakarta has also leaned toward Beijing, joining a naval exercise east of Taiwan.

mkt:tse.standing: Asia’s largest exchange, and the first major market to price each trading day.
mkt:tse.recent: The index sits near the middle of a wide 65-day range, recovering from its Jul 29 low of 61,430 after a Jun 25 peak of 72,370, and the day's move was a flat 0.21%. Nothing in the Japanese news of the period explains the swing: the Kuril Islands dispute with Russia, Chiba's record rainfall and Okinawa's base vote are political rather than market events.

mkt:hkex.standing: Where mainland Chinese companies meet foreign capital — the clearest daily read on sentiment toward China.
mkt:hkex.recent: The index has recovered most of its June drop, when it fell to 22,670 on Jun 26 from a high of 26,040 on Jun 2. Hong Kong remains the fundraising venue of choice for mainland-linked firms: Shein is raising $1.77 billion here even as the US reviews it, and Standard Chartered has begun distributing the city's dollar stablecoin.

mkt:sse.standing: Mainland China’s main board. Largely closed to foreign investors, so it tracks domestic policy more than global risk appetite.
mkt:sse.recent: The index has drifted about 4% lower over the window, from a 4,163 high on Jun 22 to a 3,764 low on Jul 17, with no single domestic shock behind the slide. The regulatory news in this period was targeted rather than macro: Beijing ordered a recall of 3 million Teslas over flush door handles and moved to draft its own supply-chain and due-diligence standards for export.

mkt:krx.standing: Dominated by Samsung and SK Hynix — a proxy for the global semiconductor cycle.
mkt:krx.recent: The Bank of Korea hiked to 3.00% on 27 August, a back-to-back move to curb inflation risks, and the index rose 1.9% on the day — well off the 22 June high of 9115 and still down 15.7% over the window. Seoul is also carrying an $880 billion AI and HBM buildout, and Washington's cancelled Twin Dragons drill.

mkt:bse.standing: Asia’s oldest exchange, founded 1875, and the benchmark for Indian equities.
mkt:bse.recent: The index sits near the top of its range after a run of policy news out of New Delhi: the government moved to privatise 11 airports in five paired bundles, and Piyush Goyal took 200 firms to Tokyo to secure semiconductor inputs. The drift back from the Aug 6 high has been slight — a 0.09% fall on the day.

mkt:sgx.standing: Southeast Asia’s financial hub, weighted to banks and regional property.
mkt:sgx.recent: The index has climbed 13.93% over the past 64 days to a high of 5768 on Aug 17, with Singapore's role as a regional financial hub in evidence: crypto card spending tripled to $1.04 billion, and a 70-member Indian delegation arrived on Aug 19 for talks on tech, investment and trade ties.

mkt:twse.standing: TSMC alone is roughly a third of the index, which makes this the most concentrated major market on the map.
mkt:twse.recent: The index recovered from its Jul 30 low of 39,930 as chip news dominated: Taiwan indicted nine people, including an Nvidia manager, over AI server smuggling, and Xiaomi launched its own Xring O3 chip to challenge Qualcomm. Pressure on the island continued, with China's coast guard now patrolling east of Taiwan.

mkt:set.standing: Thailand’s benchmark, sensitive to tourism flows and regional energy prices.
mkt:set.recent: The index sits near the top of its 38-day range after climbing from a 1541 low on Jun 23 to 1639 on Jul 17, though it fell about 2% on the latest session. Bangkok's diplomatic realignment toward Moscow has been the running story, with Russia-Thailand trade up 23% in January-May 2026 and a Thai deputy prime minister seeking cybersecurity cooperation with Russia.

mkt:pse.standing: A small, domestically-driven market where remittance flows move the index.
mkt:pse.recent: The index has climbed to 6404, roughly 7% above its late-May low, even as Manila politics dominated the headlines: an ex-disbursing officer testified that Duterte ordered a P125-million transfer of confidential funds, and the Senate impeachment court granted a witness's request for leave. The coverage offers no market-moving cause for the rise itself.

mkt:asx.standing: Mining and banking. Often the first major market to react to Chinese demand data.
mkt:asx.recent: The index reached 9,272 on Aug 6 before easing to 9,043, a 0.9% daily fall. The pullback follows a run into inflation data that traders were positioned ahead of on Aug 18, and lands alongside a weak patch for professional services in Sydney, where KPMG Australia is cutting 27 partners and 360 staff.

mkt:jse.standing: Africa’s largest exchange by far, and the continent’s only one with a usable public daily series.

mkt:b3.standing: Latin America’s largest exchange, driven by iron ore, oil and Brazilian rates.
mkt:b3.recent: The index gave up about a percentage point over the window, sliding to its Aug 18 low of 166,300 from an Aug 3 high of 178,000 before steadying near 174,600. Petrobras detected signs of oil off the Amazon coast on Aug 17, with Lula calling the equatorial margin find a "passport" for Brazil.

mkt:bmv.standing: Mexico’s benchmark, tightly coupled to US demand and the peso.
mkt:bmv.recent: The index sits roughly 3% below its late-May level, bottoming at 63,930 on Aug 18 in a stretch marked by friction with Washington: the US cancelled Andrés Manuel López Beltrán's visa on Aug 14, and Claudia Sheinbaum publicly condemned the revocation. It has since recovered to 66,290.

mkt:byma.standing: Priced in a currency that has lost most of its value repeatedly, so the index rises even in bad years. Direction over a day means something; the level does not.
mkt:byma.recent: The index has drifted rather than broken, sitting near its 63-day low of 2,874,000 on Aug 19 after peaking at 3,380,000 on Jul 22. Nothing in the Buenos Aires news window explains the move: the arrests reported there were an Interpol fraud sweep and the detention of a Milei adviser over the shooting of a lawyer, neither of which touches the listed market.

mkt:tsx.standing: Energy, mining and banks — a commodity index wearing an equity index’s clothes.
mkt:tsx.recent: The index reached 36960 on Aug 25 even as the trade fight escalated: talks with Washington collapsed and Ottawa answered with matching tariffs of up to 50% on about C$27.6bn of American goods, taxing perfume, golf clubs and video consoles. Ontario Premier Doug Ford backed retaliation, threatening to cut power exports.

mkt:nyse.standing: The largest equity market on earth. Its close sets the tone every other market opens against.
mkt:nyse.recent: The index sits near the top of its two-month range, about 2 percent above where it began and just off the 7,799 high of Aug 13, having barely moved on the day. The trade and sanctions news of the past week — Canada matching US tariffs on consumer goods, and Treasury Secretary Bessent's "Economic Outcast" campaign against Iran — has not dislodged it.

mkt:lse.standing: Most FTSE 100 revenue is earned abroad, so a falling pound tends to push the index up.
mkt:lse.recent: The index has climbed about 3.7% over the window, reaching a high of 10,910 on Jul 29 before easing to 10,880. The material here does not explain what drove the move.

mkt:xetra.standing: Germany’s industrial and chemical base — Europe’s clearest export barometer.
mkt:xetra.recent: The index sits near its 67-day peak of 26,440 on Aug 14, and the coverage in that window is mostly non-market: the EU's plan for its broadest Russia sanctions package, a second Nord Stream arrest in Croatia, and a malaria death among Frankfurt Airport workers. None of that explains the 4.4% climb from the Jun 10 low.

mkt:euronext-paris.standing: Luxury goods and energy dominate — unusually exposed to Chinese consumer demand.
mkt:euronext-paris.recent: The index sits near the top of its 67-day range, having risen from 8,147 on Jun 1 to a high of 8,726 on Aug 10 before easing to 8,462. Nothing in the Paris news of the period explains the move: the stories were regulatory and institutional — a court striking down the under-15 social media ban, a cold-call consent rule, crypto migration under MiCA — none of them market-moving for the listed 40.

mkt:euronext-amsterdam.standing: The world’s oldest exchange, now carried largely by ASML.
mkt:euronext-amsterdam.recent: The index has climbed to 1108, roughly 5% higher across the window, with the peak of 1120 on 13 August and no single Dutch event in view to explain the run. The daily move is flat, down 0.145%.

mkt:bme.standing: Spanish banks with heavy Latin American exposure make this a proxy for both regions.
mkt:bme.recent: The index has climbed roughly a tenth over the past 67 days, reaching a high of 20,210 on Aug 11 after a low of 18,140 on Jun 10. The clearest domestic input in that stretch was Spain's decision to extend the life of its largest nuclear plant, a policy U-turn that lands directly on the utilities carrying much of the index's weight.

mkt:borsa-italiana.standing: Banks and utilities, and the market most sensitive to Italian sovereign debt spreads.
mkt:borsa-italiana.recent: The index sits near the top of its 67-day range, having climbed about 5% from its late-May low of 49,580 to a high of 53,720 on Aug 7 and holding close to that since. Nothing in the available material explains the move.

mkt:six.standing: Nestlé, Roche and Novartis carry the index, which makes it defensive when the world turns risk-off.

mkt:nasdaq-stockholm.standing: Nordic industrials and telecoms, and a useful early read on European capital spending.
mkt:nasdaq-stockholm.recent: The index sits near the top of its range, up 5.7% over the window and 1% on the day, after a high of 3327 on Aug 5. The available material does not explain the move.

mkt:tase.standing: Trades Sunday to Thursday. Heavily weighted to banks, defence and technology.
mkt:tase.recent: The index is down 8.5% across the 66-day window, sliding from a high of 4433 on May 27 to a low of 3966 on Jun 29. It has clawed back part of that ground since, sitting at 4043. Nothing in the available material explains the decline.

xag.standing: A digital token backed one-for-one by physical silver, quoted per ounce. Silver trades as both a monetary hedge and an industrial input — solar cells, electronics and brazing all consume it — so its price answers to two different buyers.
xag.recent: The month has swung rather than trended: a low of $29.80 on Aug 6, a high of $67.31 on Aug 20, and a latest reading of $45.82, roughly a fifth below where the window opened. Nothing in the available record explains the swings.

poly-will-there-be-no-change-in-fed-inte.standing: A Polymarket contract on whether the Federal Reserve leaves its policy rate unchanged at its next meeting. The price is what traders will pay for that outcome, so it moves as the case for a cut or a hike is made and unmade.
poly-will-there-be-no-change-in-fed-inte.recent: The contract has climbed from 39% on Aug 1 to 68%, peaking at 75% on Aug 15. Fed minutes released on Aug 19 showed many officials said rate hikes may be needed, which cuts against a cut without making one likely, and traders looked past CPI to the Fed's next tests.

poly-us-x-iran-ceasefire-continues-throu.standing: A Polymarket contract on whether the US–Iran ceasefire holds to a set date. Traders buy and sell the outcome, so the price is what people will pay for the ceasefire surviving — a running read on how close the two sides are to shooting again.
poly-us-x-iran-ceasefire-continues-throu.recent: The price climbed from 83 on Aug 19 to 96 as Washington moved the confrontation onto financial ground: Treasury Secretary Bessent named the campaign "Economic Outcast" and designated nearly 60 entities, sanctions rather than strikes. Iran and Oman then agreed a temporary corridor through Hormuz, even as Rezaei threatened a shutdown.

wiki-lebanon.standing: Wikipedia's Lebanon article, and how many people open it each day. Attention to a country page tends to move with events on its territory rather than with anything about the page itself, which makes the count a rough register of when the outside world turns to look.
wiki-lebanon.recent: The peak on Aug 21 sat between two Lebanon stories: families in Beirut pressing the ICC over Israeli strikes that have killed 28 journalists since 2023, and Lebanon's finding days later that glyphosate in the soil at Ayta ash-Shaab had reached 50 times normal levels. Earlier in the month a strike near Ansar destroyed a house and killed seven.

wiki-petroleum.standing: Crude oil and the fuels refined from it — the base input for transport, freight, fertiliser and much of the chemicals industry. Its price and the politics around who pumps, refines and taxes it reach almost every household through what things cost to move.
wiki-petroleum.recent: Attention tracked a fuel-politics run rather than a price. Jamaat-e-Islami emir Rehman said patience had run out and threatened a shutdown over Pakistan's petroleum levy, after diesel rose Rs6.47 to Rs390.42 a litre and a crude line burst under homes in Karachi. Putin conceded not all fuel issues have been resolved.

poly-will-the-us-invade-iran-before-2027.standing: A Polymarket contract on whether the United States launches a military invasion of Iran before 2027. The price is what traders will pay for that outcome, so it moves with each turn between confrontation and negotiation.
poly-will-the-us-invade-iran-before-2027.recent: The odds fell from 26 on Aug 2 to 16 as Washington chose money over missiles: Treasury Secretary Bessent named a sanctions campaign "Economic Outcast," designating nearly 60 entities and binding third countries. Iran and Oman then agreed a temporary corridor through the Strait of Hormuz, and Trump called Munir before his Tehran trip.

wiki-syria.standing: The Wikipedia article on Syria, and the number of people who open it each day. Reader attention to a country tracks what the world is being told about it, and it rises fastest when the news is bad or the politics change.
wiki-syria.recent: The rise tracked Syria's reopening to the outside world. On 18 August Syria granted the IAEA access to an Assad-era undeclared nuclear site concealed for 18 years, eight Israeli strikes hit an airbase in Idlib, and a court sentenced Wassim al-Assad to death. Trump then removed Syria from the terrorism list on 24 August.

wiki-donald-trump.standing: The English Wikipedia article on the 45th and 47th President of the United States. Its daily readership is one of the steadiest proxies for how much of the world is looking at Washington on any given day.
wiki-donald-trump.recent: The month's traffic tracked a run of Trump decisions abroad: Kushner's meetings with Hamas and then Netanyahu to push a Gaza plan, the delisting of Syria after 47 years on the terror list, and a widened sanctions push on Iran that Gulf states have not welcomed. At home, the Supreme Court denied his appeal in the Carroll case without comment.

poly-will-renan-santos-win-the-2026-braz.standing: A Polymarket contract on a candidate's chances in Brazil's 2026 presidential race, priced in cents on the dollar. It is not a poll and not a forecast — it is what traders are willing to pay for that outcome, and it reprices the moment the field changes.
poly-will-renan-santos-win-the-2026-braz.recent: The contract has fallen by two thirds over the month, from 10% on Jul 28 to 3% by Aug 23, where it has stayed. Nothing in the input explains the slide.

wiki-volodymyr-zelenskyy.standing: The president of Ukraine, elected in 2019 and leading the country through Russia's full-scale invasion. His readership rises with the war's turning points, with the arms and money his government depends on, and with the politics of his own office.
wiki-volodymyr-zelenskyy.recent: The late-July peak came and faded; the sharpest recent reading followed 19 August, when anti-corruption agents searched Zelenskyy's own office over a $3.4-million fraud probe and he fired another top ally. A Russian missile strike on Kyiv killed at least 13 the next day as air defences faltered.

stocks:XIACY.standing: A Chinese consumer-electronics maker turned carmaker: phones, home appliances and, since 2024, electric vehicles. Its shares are a read on Chinese consumer demand and on how far a hardware assembler can move up into its own silicon.
stocks:XIACY.recent: Xiaomi's Xring O3 chip, unveiled on 24 August, is an in-house AI mobile processor that challenges Qualcomm directly — a bid for design sovereignty rather than fabrication. The stock has drifted lower over the window, from $20.17 on Jul 29 to a $16.19 low on Aug 18, and the launch has not reversed it.

stocks:HPQ.standing: One of the largest makers of personal computers and printers, spun out of Hewlett-Packard in 2015. Its results track corporate PC refresh cycles and the consumables business that sells ink and toner long after the hardware ships.

stocks:BLK.standing: The world's largest asset manager, overseeing money for pension funds, governments and ordinary savers through index funds and ETFs. Its scale makes it a gatekeeper: what it lists, buys or holds shapes where trillions of dollars flow.
stocks:BLK.recent: The stock climbed through the window, from $1,062 on Jul 27 to a high of $1,183 on Aug 13, holding near $1,177 since. BlackRock cut the swap-in threshold on its bitcoin product from $25 million to $1 million, widening access to in-kind creation.

stocks:NVDA.standing: The largest designer of the graphics processors that train and run AI models, sold mostly to data-centre operators. Its order book is the closest thing to a meter on how much the world is spending to build AI infrastructure.
stocks:NVDA.recent: Nvidia beat estimates and guided to $108bn in revenue next quarter, but the run to $225.30 on Aug 13 and the pullback since track a different question: the company has pledged $500 billion to its own buyers, backstops $230 billion in customer lease obligations, and disclosed a $21 billion SpaceX stake. Taiwan also indicted nine people, including an Nvidia manager.

stocks:RVMD.standing: A US biotechnology company developing targeted cancer therapies, focused on drugs aimed at RAS proteins — mutations long considered undruggable and present in a large share of pancreatic, lung and colorectal tumours.
stocks:RVMD.recent: The stock climbed toward its high of $216 on Aug 18 and sat at $213.4 by Aug 26, when the FDA cleared daraxonrasib, a pancreatic pill that nearly doubled median survival to 13.2 months. The low of $180.9 came on Jul 29, ahead of the decision.

stocks:META.standing: Meta Platforms runs Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp, and earns almost all of its money selling advertising against the attention of billions of users. Its costs and its legal exposure both scale with how those feeds are built and who is on them.
stocks:META.recent: Two Menlo Park stories landed on 26 August: a $17.1bn settlement over social media harms to children, roughly 1% of Meta's stock value, and a report that the company drew up and then abandoned a plan to cut some teams by as much as 60% to become 'AI native'. The stock sits at $576.1, below its 11 August high of $599.1.

stocks:V.standing: One of the two dominant card networks. It neither lends nor issues cards; it runs the rails that authorise and settle card payments between banks and merchants, taking a small cut of every transaction that crosses them.
stocks:V.recent: The stock rose from 358.8 on Aug 17 to 384.1 on Aug 25, a run the window does not account for. The only company news in it is South Korea's Shinhan Financial tapping Visa to build AI and stablecoin payments, and that landed on 2026-08-26, after the peak. The other visa headlines concern travel documents, not the card network.
